rules.title: Sideways markets reward patience
rules.lesson: When price is moving sideways and implied volatility is high, short-term option buyers can lose money from time decay even if the stock does not move against them.
rules.example: If a stock stays near the same price for several days, a long call can lose value because expiration is getting closer.
rules.risk_note: Waiting for a breakout, selling premium only with defined risk, or using spreads can reduce exposure to time decay.

rules.title: Bullish views can be expressed with stock or calls
rules.lesson: Buying stock gives linear upside and downside. Buying calls gives leveraged upside but can expire worthless.
rules.example: A 5% stock rally benefits both a long stock position and a long call, but the call also depends on strike, premium, volatility, and time.
rules.risk_note: Options require direction, timing, and magnitude to be sufficiently favorable.

rules.title: Bearish trades should define risk before entry
rules.lesson: Long puts and put spreads can express downside views with defined maximum loss.
rules.example: A long put can gain if the stock falls below strike minus premium before expiration.
rules.risk_note: Short options or uncovered bearish trades can create large losses if risk is not capped.

rules.title: High implied volatility changes the trade
rules.lesson: High implied volatility makes options more expensive. Buyers need a larger move to overcome premium paid.
rules.example: A call may be directionally correct but still lose money if implied volatility drops after entry.
rules.risk_note: Compare expected move, break-even price, and position sizing before entering.

rules.title: Risk-on favors directional long exposure
rules.lesson: When volatility is falling and growth stocks lead, directional long stock, call spreads, and momentum setups tend to work better than aggressive premium selling.
rules.example: A broad rally with VIX declining often lifts calls and reduces fear premium faster than sideways income trades capture.
rules.risk_note: Do not cap upside too early with tight covered calls if you expect a sustained trend.

rules.title: Neutral markets favor structured income
rules.lesson: Choppy markets with elevated IV reward defined-risk credit structures: covered calls, put spreads, iron condors, and diagonals that harvest time decay.
rules.example: If price stays in a range for weeks, an iron condor can profit while a long straddle loses premium to theta.
rules.risk_note: Gap risk can still break ranges—size positions for loss outside the long strikes.

rules.title: Protective puts are insurance, not a trade idea
rules.lesson: A protective put limits downside on stock you already own. You pay premium for peace of mind before events or during stress.
rules.example: Stock down 10% may cost $1,000; with a put, loss can be closer to premium paid if strike is near the money.
rules.risk_note: Insurance raises break-even—only buy protection when the thesis requires holding through risk.

rules.title: Liquidity is part of the trade
rules.lesson: Wide bid/ask spreads and low open interest increase real cost. Prefer contracts with tight markets and visible volume.
rules.example: Paying $0.30 wide on a $1.00 option is a 30% round-trip handicap before the stock moves.
rules.risk_note: Use mid prices for estimates but assume fills near bid when selling and ask when buying.

rules.title: Credit spreads do not need max profit
rules.lesson: Closing credit spreads at 50–80% of maximum profit reduces gamma risk into expiration.
rules.example: A spread opened for $2.00 credit might be closed for $0.50 debit instead of waiting for full decay.
rules.risk_note: Always close both legs together with a combo order when possible.
